How Adult Platforms Can Prepare for California's AB 1705 Requirements

Corey Silverstein Nov 17, 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 7:36
Instaread

California’s AB 1705 takes effect Jan. 1, 2027, giving adult website operators a short runway to prepare. Signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom on Sept. 30, the law creates new obligations involving uploader verification, age and consent certifications, record retention and content already displayed on covered websites.

Meeting those requirements will involve legal, engineering, moderation and content teams. Here is what operators need to know about who is covered, what information they must collect and preserve, how existing libraries may be affected and what liability they could face for falling short.

Businesses based outside California should still ask counsel whether their activities create a connection to the state. Incorporating or hosting servers elsewhere, or attempting to block California access, may not settle the question.

Who Is Covered?

AB 1705 applies to any “pornographic internet website” that allows users to upload, or asks them to provide, sexually explicit content for display. Because the law defines a user as either a person or an entity, operators should consider content received from creators, studios and distributors, along with material submitted through public upload tools. The law does not set a minimum threshold for revenue, traffic or the percentage of explicit content hosted.

The scope has limits. Content with serious literary, artistic or scientific value is excluded, as are services used solely for email, direct messaging, cloud storage, file transfer or collaboration. Sexually explicit content shared privately between selected users of a dating service may also be excluded, provided it does not appear publicly, in a public feed or in search results. That exclusion applies to qualifying private communications, not the dating platform as a whole.

Businesses based outside California should still ask counsel whether their activities create a connection to the state. Incorporating or hosting servers elsewhere, or attempting to block California access, may not settle the question.

What Uploaders Must Certify

Although “depicted individual” sounds like a general term, AB 1705 uses it more narrowly. It refers to someone shown nude or engaging in sexual acts who did not consent to being depicted, was a minor when the content was created or did not consent to the upload.

Those distinctions matter. Confirming someone is an adult today does not establish that they were an adult when the content was made. Likewise, consenting to appear in content is different from consenting to its upload. Ownership or distribution rights do not necessarily resolve either question.

Before allowing someone to upload sexually explicit content, an operator must verify that user’s email address. Simply collecting the address or sending a welcome message is not enough. A verification link or code is one practical option. Whatever method the operator chooses must cover every submission route, including mobile interfaces, application programming interfaces, bulk imports, partner dashboards and existing accounts.

For each upload, the user must certify under penalty of perjury that everyone depicted was an adult when the content was created, consented to being depicted and consented to the upload. The user must also provide contact information that includes at least an email address.

Counsel should draft certification language that clearly addresses all three points, since a general promise to follow the law may not be sufficient. Each certification should also be connected to the files it covers, including every file submitted in a batch.

Knowingly providing false information is an infraction punishable by a $1,000 fine. If an operator fails to obtain the required statement, the law presumes that the operator violated its duty concerning displayed content.

Even a properly completed certification does not provide blanket protection. Operators must still exercise ordinary care and reasonable diligence. Credible concerns involving age, consent or the uploader’s authority should be escalated and, when appropriate, the content should be held for further review.

Records, Libraries and Complaints

Operators must retain each certification and the uploader’s contact information in a readily available format for at least seven years. That period begins when the information is submitted, regardless of when the content is removed or the account is closed.

Existing deletion practices may therefore need to change. Removing a video, closing an account or migrating to another system should not erase required records. Each certification should be linked to the submission date, uploader information and relevant content, then protected through secure storage and reliable recovery procedures.

Older content also deserves attention. AB 1705 contains no express exception for material uploaded before the law takes effect. That does not make a pre-2027 upload retroactively unlawful, but continuing to display it after Jan. 1 may create exposure.

Operators should inventory their content sources and prioritize material associated with unresolved complaints, missing documentation or unidentified suppliers. The law does not expressly require a new certification for every historical upload, so counsel should evaluate how it applies to specific legacy content.

Complaints involving age or consent should reach someone authorized to investigate and act. Although AB 1705 does not establish a universal hourly takedown deadline, leaving potentially unlawful content accessible can increase the risk. Removal procedures should address thumbnails, previews, alternate URLs and cached copies rather than only the main content page.

Understanding the Exposure

A depicted individual harmed by a covered violation may sue the website operator and, under certain conditions, the uploader. A successful plaintiff may recover actual damages or statutory damages of up to $75,000 per violation, whichever is greater. The court may also award punitive damages, attorney’s fees and costs, an injunction and other available relief.

The $75,000 figure is not automatic, nor does it represent a universal limit on total exposure. Public prosecutors may separately seek civil penalties of $25,000 per violation, along with equitable relief, attorney’s fees and costs. Each full calendar day that unlawfully uploaded or displayed content remains accessible counts as a separate violation.

Contracts with suppliers and vendors should address documentation, the accuracy of submitted information, cooperation with investigations and responses to age or consent disputes. Operators that rely on outside upload or moderation services should also know exactly what those vendors verify and retain, how quickly records can be retrieved and what remains available after the relationship ends.

The Road to Jan. 1

Management should begin by appointing a compliance lead and asking counsel to assess how the law applies to the business. From there, teams can map every submission channel, inventory existing content, implement email verification and certification controls, establish retention rules, update supplier procedures and train employees to handle potential problems.

Once those systems are in place, test the complete process. Retrieve a certification and connect it to the relevant content. Send a mock complaint through the escalation process, then confirm that authorized employees can disable every accessible copy.

These are recommended preparation steps, not deadlines imposed by the statute. Counsel should continue monitoring amendments, court orders and other developments. Unless a court orders otherwise, however, operators should not assume that a legal challenge will delay the compliance deadline.

By Jan. 1, operators should be able to explain how content enters their platforms, what uploaders certified, how required records are preserved and how age or consent concerns are addressed. For businesses that still need to build that framework, late December will be far too late to begin.
